III. **The Axiom of Excluded Middle**: "Everything must either be or not be; there is no other alternative or middle course."

These are established <term>axioms</term> <note>Self-evident truths or fundamental principles that serve as the starting point for all logical reasoning.</note> of Logic. A leading authority, Prof. Jevons <note>William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882) was an influential English logician and economist whose works were standard textbooks in the late 19th century.</note>, says of them: "Students are seldom able to see at first their full meaning and importance. All arguments may be explained when these self-evident laws are granted; and it is not too much to say that the whole of Logic will be plain to those who will constantly use these laws as the key."

Therefore, we must either hold that the Cosmos is under Law and Order, or else that it is not. And if it is not, then Chance or an <term>Arbitrary Decree</term> <note>A decision made by a ruler based on whim rather than established rules or reason.</note> rules the universe—and the Cosmos is merely Chaos. There is no alternative—there can be no "half-and-half" middle ground in this matter. Which is it? 

We hardly need to assure the student that the highest modern scientific thought agrees perfectly with the teachings of the ancient <term>occultists</term> <note>Here referring to those who study the "hidden" or underlying laws of nature and reality.</note>: that the Cosmos is governed by Law in every detail and as a whole, and that universal order, balance, and harmony are manifested through it. Not only is this true, but the ordinary human mind is capable of discovering the existence of Law in the universe in every way it manifests. The rising of the sun, the flow of the tides, the law of gravitation, the laws of mechanics, and "Natural Law" in all its forms show that Law exists in the Cosmos. 

Science shows us that the entire universe is held together by the operation of Law. If the tiniest atom were released from the operation of Law, the entire universe would dissolve into Chaos; its parts are so interdependent that even the slightest exception to Universal Law would be inconsistent with the whole system. The Laws of the Universe can never be "broken." If we come into contact with them and refuse to govern ourselves accordingly, we suffer—but the Law remains intact. We do not "break" the Law of Gravitation when we step over a cliff; we only prove its existence. If we could "break" even the smallest Law of the Cosmos, the Cosmos would become Chaos.

Furthermore, these Cosmic Laws are not the result of an arbitrary <term>fiat</term> <note>original: "fiat", a Latin word meaning "let it be done"; an authoritative decree.</note> or <term>dictum</term> <note>original: "dictum", a Latin word for a formal pronouncement or command.</note> of some Being. Instead, they are inherent in the very nature of—

translation:
### XVII.
Arbitrators have the obligation imposed upon them to impose an end to the entire controversy by their sentence, but not the liberty to test whether the parties might allow the dispute to be settled by their counsel or authority.

### XVIII.
They are bound by this necessity only if a penalty—whether monetary or another thing instead of money, whether a fixed sum or uncertain, or whether greater or lesser than the matter in question—has been promised unconditionally, not conditionally, by the parties involved in the compromise, should anyone fail to abide by the arbitrators' sentence.

### XIX.
To this end, the magistrate or ordinary judge is accustomed to interpose his authority so that the arbitrators perform the duty they voluntarily accepted at the beginning in a timely manner.

### XX.
Hence, if the arbitrators attempt to conceal themselves, the magistrate must track them down, and if they do not appear for a long time, he ought to impose a fine against them.

### XXI.
The parties who made the compromise must abide by the sentence of the arbitrators rendered within the established time, whether it is just or unjust, provided it was not rendered contrary to the laws and sacred Constitutions, for fear of the penalty.

### XXII.
Indeed, it is convenient for the sentence to be pronounced in the presence of the litigants: unless it was specifically expressed in the compromise that it be pronounced in the absence of one or both; if this is not done, the absent party incurs the penalty, unless they are prepared to compromise again before the same agreeing arbitrator.

### XXIII.
The penalty from the compromise is sought from the one who has not obeyed the sentence of the arbitrators.

<summary>These conclusions address the arbitrator’s duty to reach a final decision, the role of the magistrate in enforcing their presence, and the requirement for parties to adhere to the final sentence.</summary>

### Here is the <term>Svalpajataka</term> <gloss>Little Book of Birth</gloss>:

**"Here, etc."**: The subsequent verse is from another work. (43)

**"Whichever, etc."**: By the word "etc.," connections through trines and the like should be understood. The connection with the ascendant is the presence of the lord of the house in the ascendant, in an angle from it, or by its aspect. Otherwise, only the connection of the houses with the ascendant is certain. (43)

**"Of the planets, etc."**: They are spoken of in two verses. (44)

**"For benefics, etc."**: "Abhimati" is the enemy, the sixth house. Among these twelve houses. "Dharmatmaja" are the ninth and fifth. Among these three—the ascendant, the fifth, and the ninth—the auspicious or inauspicious result is the auspicious result for the good, and the inauspicious result for the bad. When the ascendant, fifth, and ninth are associated with benefics, there is prosperity even for other houses like wealth. When those three have malefic influences, there is generally a loss of others, is the meaning. (44)

**"Copper, etc."**: Even though it is stated that malefics are favorable in the sixth house, in the case of questions about disease and the like, they are unfavorable. This means they are auspicious in questions regarding work and the like. (45)

**"Here, etc."**: Here, in the matter of contemplating the house.

They certainly honored memory very much and applied great exercise and care to it. In learning, they would not let go of what was being taught until they had firmly grasped the things of the first lesson, and they practiced recollection of things said daily in the following manner. (165) A Pythagorean man did not rise from his bed before he had recollected the events of the previous day. He performed the recollection in this way: he tried to recover in his mind what he first said or heard or ordered for the household after rising, and what was second, and what was third. The same logic applied to subsequent events. And again, upon going out, whom he first met and whom second, and what words were spoken first, second, and third; and the same logic for all other things. For he tried to recover in his mind everything that happened in the whole day, desiring to remember them in the order in which each of them happened to occur. If he had more leisure upon waking, he tried to recover the events of the third day in the same way. (166) They tried even more to exercise the memory, for nothing is greater for knowledge, experience, and wisdom than the ability to remember. From these practices, it happened that all of Italy was filled with philosopher men, and though it was previously unknown, it was later called Great Greece because of Pythagoras, and many philosophers, poets, and lawmakers arose among them. For the rhetorical arts, the demonstration speeches, and the written laws were brought from them into Greece. And regarding natural philosophers, whoever makes mention of them, they happen to bring forward Empedocles and Parmenides the Eleatic first; and those wishing to say something wise about life bring forward the thoughts of Epicharmus, and almost all philosophers possess them. <note>Regarding section 163, compare Cramer's notes: the Pythagoreans, as Aristoxenus said, used purification of the body through medicine and of the soul through music. Everything they define regarding acting or not acting is aimed at communion with the divine; this is the starting principle, and their whole life is organized toward following God. The logic of this philosophy is that men act ridiculously when seeking the good from anywhere other than from the gods. It is similar to a person in a kingdom who serves a minor official of the citizens but neglects the ruler and king of all. For they think humans do such a thing. Since there is a God and He is the lord of all, and it is agreed that one must ask the lord for the good—and everyone gives good things to those they love and in whom they delight, but the opposite to those they are against—it is clear that those things must be done in which God happens to delight.
